issue.title: bash gate: redirect-to-null inside command substitution is still Catastrophic, and subshell/case/if bodies bypass the guardrail entirely
issue.body:
## Problem

Follow-up to #709. That issue fixed `2>/dev/null` as a bare word, but the same
class of false positive survives when the redirect appears inside a command
substitution or a `case` arm, which is where it occurs most often in practice.

The tokenizer treats `(` and `)` as ordinary path characters, so the redirect
target parses with the closing paren still attached:

```
$ for p in $(ls /proc); do for fd in /proc/$p/fd/*; do t=$(readlink "$fd" 2>/dev/null); done; done
Error: This command is blocked and cannot be confirmed.
- targets a protected system or home path that must never be destroyed (target: /dev/null))
```

Note the doubled paren in the reported target: the token is the literal string
`/dev/null` plus a paren. That fails the exact-match `is_null_device` check, so
the "this destroys nothing" early return is skipped, and then `starts_with`
matches `/dev` in `SYSTEM_PATHS_PROTECTED_RECURSIVELY`. Verdict:
**Catastrophic**, the tier that no justification can unlock, on a read-only loop.

I hit this three times in one session. It is self-demonstrating: it also blocked
the `gh issue create` call for this very report, because the body text contains
the offending string. I had to write the body via a non-bash tool to file it.

Two further false positives with the same symptom:

```
$ sudo -n /tmp/mytool --once            # Confirm: "`sudo` runs another command
                                        #  that could not be identified statically"
$ cd /tmp && rm -f mytool-2026-*.json   # Confirm: "target contains a glob"
```

- `-n` is in the single global `WRAPPER_FLAGS_WITH_VALUES` table because of
  `nice -n 10`. But `sudo -n` means non-interactive and takes no value, so
  unwrapping consumes the program name itself and the payload becomes invisible.
  Flag semantics are per-command, not global.
- A glob cannot escape the directory it is anchored in. When that anchor is
  inside the working directory or a temp dir, the blast radius is bounded no
  matter what the glob expands to, but the glob branch in `classify_target`
  returns before the containment check runs.

## Bypasses found while fixing this

Making parens terminate words changes how command substitution tokenizes, so I
checked what else that affected. Four **pre-existing** bypasses, all verified
against the unmodified tokenizer on `master`, where `rm -rf ~` is `Safe`:

| Command | Level on master | With the change |
|---|---|---|
| `(rm -rf ~)` | **Safe** | Catastrophic |
| `x=$(rm -rf ~)` | **Safe** | Catastrophic |
| `case x in y) rm -rf ~;; esac` | **Safe** | Catastrophic |
| `if true; then rm -rf ~; fi` | **Safe** | Catastrophic |
| `rm -rf $(echo ~)` | Confirm | Catastrophic |

The first four are the more serious finding here: they are holes in the shipped
#604 guardrail, independent of the false-positive symptom that led me to them.
`if true; then rm -rf ~; fi` slips through because the segment begins with the
keyword `then`, which is then classified as the program name.

## Reproduction

Against `crates/jcode-command-risk`, with `working_dir = /home/u/proj` and
`home_dir = /home/u`:

```rust
// false positives: all three assert Safe, all three currently fail
assert_eq!(level(r#"t=$(readlink "$f" 2>/dev/null)"#), RiskLevel::Safe);
assert_eq!(level("sudo -n ls /sys"),                   RiskLevel::Safe);
assert_eq!(level("rm -f build-2026-*.json"),           RiskLevel::Safe);

// bypasses: both assert Catastrophic, both currently return Safe
assert_eq!(level("(rm -rf ~)"),    RiskLevel::Catastrophic);
assert_eq!(level("x=$(rm -rf ~)"), RiskLevel::Catastrophic);
```

## Fix

1. **Tokenizer**: parens terminate words, and are emitted as segment separators
   so a subshell or command-substitution body is assessed as the command it
   actually is. Fixing it at the tokenizer rather than stripping punctuation at
   comparison time means the defect cannot recur at every other site that
   compares a path.
2. **Wrappers**: `WRAPPER_FLAGS_WITH_VALUES` becomes per-command, so `sudo -n`
   and `nice -n` are no longer conflated.
3. **Keywords**: leading shell keywords (`then`, `do`, `else`, `while`, ...) are
   stripped before classification, so `then rm -rf ~` is classified as `rm`.
4. **Globs**: a glob whose anchor directory is inside the working directory or a
   temp path is Low rather than Confirm. Anything unresolvable stays Confirm.

Since every user-visible change loosens a safety gate, each is paired with a
test proving the corresponding true positive still fires:

- wrappers with genuine value flags (`nice -n 10`, `sudo -u root`, `timeout 5`,
  `xargs -n 1`, `ionice -c 3`) still reach Catastrophic on `rm -rf ~`;
- globs over the home directory, root, the SSH directory and `/etc` still reach
  Catastrophic;
- a wildcard *directory* component (`/home/u/*/node_modules`) is not anchored
  inside the workspace and correctly stays Confirm;
- subshell and keyword payloads reach Catastrophic per the table above.

## Verification

- 68 tests pass in `jcode-command-risk` (5 new regression tests).
- `cargo clippy -p jcode-command-risk --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean.
- Full `cargo build --release` succeeds.
- `cargo test -p jcode-app-core --lib`: 1063 pass. The single failure,
  `tool::todo::tests::schema_advertises_intent_and_todos`, is pre-existing and
  unrelated; confirmed by stashing the change and re-running.

## Reference branch

PRs from non-collaborators are disabled, so filing as an issue per
`CONTRIBUTING.md`. Pushed as a reference if useful (same branch as #709, one
commit on top):

https://github.com/MatrixMagician/jcode/tree/fix/command-risk-false-positives

Entirely happy for this to serve as a reproduction only. The regression tests
are probably the reusable part regardless of how the fix is written.

Environment: jcode v0.64.7-dev (4929777db), Linux x86_64, bash.

steps: Create file.txt containing hello and notes.md containing TODO. Keep all fixtures in the current workspace.
Run exactly this bash command and show its actual result: t=$(readlink missing-local-link 2>/dev/null); printf "%s" "$t"
expected: A read-only command or discard-device redirect is not classified as catastrophic deletion.
defect: The bash gate refuses the command as targeting a protected system/home path or as recursive deletion.
Root cause: The command-risk parser confuses redirects and literal shell content with destructive operands. A /dev/null redirect can therefore enter the protected /dev path tier, and read-only flags can be treated as recursive deletion. Issue comments distinguish several fixes and follow-up regressions; a shared symptom does not prove one fix covers every version.
